pages.text: Selikem’s cousin worked in a small-scale gold mine and had been chased from a pit twice. “Sir,” Selikem asked his geography teacher, Mr Tsikata, “has any country fixed this problem?” Mr Tsikata unrolled a world map and pinned four countries. “No country has fixed it completely,” he said. “But some have tried sensible things, and some have stumbled. Let us learn from both.”
sentences: Selikem’s cousin worked in a small-scale gold mine and had been chased from a pit twice.
“Sir,” Selikem asked his geography teacher, Mr Tsikata, “has any country fixed this problem?” Mr Tsikata unrolled a world map and pinned four countries.
“No country has fixed it completely,” he said.
“But some have tried sensible things, and some have stumbled.
Let us learn from both.”
pages.alt: A boy asks a question in class while a teacher pins four countries on a world map.

pages.text: “Peru, in South America,” said Mr Tsikata. “In 2002, Peru passed a law for small and artisanal miners. It gave clear groups, lower fees, simpler environmental permits and a path to become legal. A 2012 study called the best cases the most successful it had seen. But the study also found problems. The government never gave the support it promised. Small miners had to dig a minimum amount each year. And they were not allowed to hire each other.”
sentences: “Peru, in South America,” said Mr Tsikata.
“In 2002, Peru passed a law for small and artisanal miners.
It gave clear groups, lower fees, simpler environmental permits and a path to become legal.
A 2012 study called the best cases the most successful it had seen.
But the study also found problems.
The government never gave the support it promised.
Small miners had to dig a minimum amount each year.
And they were not allowed to hire each other.”
pages.alt: A teacher points to Peru on a map beside a sketch of a law book and a gold scale.

pages.text: “There was a bright spot,” Mr Tsikata continued. “A Peruvian miners’ cooperative called SOTRAMI won a Fairmined label. Fairmined means the gold was mined responsibly, and buyers pay extra. The study listed benefits such as legal status, social security and ten to fifteen per cent more money. But the study is from 2012, so the figures may be different today.” Selikem wrote: good example, old date, check.

pages.text: “Tanzania, in East Africa,” said Mr Tsikata. “The study says that licences were hard to get and the licence lasted seven years, with no promise of renewal. Some sites were too small. But there was practical help. A university gave twenty miners a retort, a closed container that catches mercury vapour so it can be used again. Eighteen miners used it for five months and saved about ten kilograms of mercury.”

pages.text: “Ecuador,” said Mr Tsikata, “passed a law in 1992 that made lawful the mines already working. That helped many miners to become legal. But permits could not be passed on, banks did not lend, and the training did not last. In Mongolia, mercury was banned in 2008, but the study says some people still use it in secret.” Selikem frowned. “So a law alone does not do the job,” he said. “Exactly,” said Mr Tsikata.

pages.text: Together, the class made two lists on the board. What helped: clear categories, simple permits, legal recognition, groups and cooperatives, certification with a premium, practical training with tools. What fell short: weak government support, costs that differ by region, rules that blocked cooperation, no credit for formal miners, and bans without enforcement or alternatives. “These are lessons, not recipes,” said Mr Tsikata. “Ghana has its own laws and its own forests. Borrow ideas, do not copy blindly.”

pages.text: Mr Tsikata set a question: should Ghana make licences cheaper and quicker for small groups? Selikem wrote: “Some people argue that cheaper and quicker licences would bring more miners into the law, where they can be trained and checked. However, others argue that if checking is weak, more licences could mean more damage to forests and water. The Peruvian example shows that guidance without force is often ignored. Therefore, in my view, licences should be quicker only if training, inspection and land restoration are properly supported.”

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: an argumentative paragraph states the question, gives one side with evidence, gives the other side, and then gives a reasoned conclusion. Selikem used “some people argue”, “however” and “therefore”, named his evidence instead of presenting it as unquestionable fact, and avoided contractions and slang. Check that your evidence is attributed and dated. The end.
